Rav Pappa derives it from the verse 'he and his sons among Israel', applying in peacetime without anointing.

Why not explain it as Jehu being the first of his dynasty, rather than due to the dispute?
The baraita is incomplete and its actual teaching is that kings of Judah are anointed and kings of Israel are not.
The rule is restated: kings of the house of David are anointed, while kings of Israel are not.
From where do we derive this?
Rava cites 1 Samuel 16:12, 'arise, anoint him, for this is he', showing only David required anointing.
The Master says Jehu was anointed only due to Joram's dispute.
Shall we misuse consecrated anointing oil on a king of Israel who does not require it?
As Rav Pappa said, they anointed him with pure balsam oil, not with the sacred anointing oil.
Jehoahaz was anointed because of Jehoiakim, who was two years older than him.
But was Jehoiakim older than Jehoahaz?
1 Chronicles 3:15 lists the sons of Josiah in order, with Jehoiakim second and Zedekiah third.
Rabbi Yoḥanan identifies the names: Shallum is Zedekiah, and Johanan is Jehoahaz.
Jehoiakim was in fact older, and firstborn refers to Jehoahaz's status for ascending the throne.
Do younger sons rule before elder ones?
2 Chronicles 21:3 says the kingdom went to Jehoram because he was the firstborn.
Jehoram was suited to his ancestors' role, unlike Jehoiakim, so the younger brother ascended first.
The Master repeats the identifications: Shallum is Zedekiah, Johanan is Jehoahaz.
But the verse lists them separately, third and fourth, so they seem to be different people.
Third means among the sons, and fourth means in succession to the throne, in the order of reigns.
A baraita states that Shallum is Zedekiah.
Why was he named Shallum?
Some say the name refers to the Davidic kingdom being completed during his days.
What was his actual name?
His name was Mattaniah.
2 Kings 24:17 is cited: the king of Babylon made Mattaniah king and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Nebuchadnezzar renamed him, saying God would justify judgment against him if he rebelled.
2 Kings 25:7 and 2 Chronicles 36:13 support that he was taken to Babylon after rebelling against the oath.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Was there anointing oil in Jehoahaz's time, given a baraita that says it was sequestered with the Ark?
Josiah sequestered the sacred objects, including the Ark.
Josiah saw in Deuteronomy 28:36 that the Ark would be taken into exile, so he hid it.
Second Chronicles 35:3 is cited, showing that the Levites were told to place the Ark in Solomon's Temple.
Rabbi Elazar uses verbal analogies to show that all these items were sequestered together.
Rav Pappa says they anointed Jehoahaz with pure balsam oil, not the sacred oil.
A baraita describes how kings are anointed, in a crown-like shape, and how priests are anointed.
What is meant by the shape being like the Greek letter chi?
Rav Menashya bar Gadda explains that the shape is like the Greek form of the letter kaf.
Two baraitot disagree on whether anointing or pouring oil comes first; the tanna'im dispute which is preferable.
What is the reasoning of the one who holds that pouring is preferable?
Leviticus 8:12 says he poured the oil on Aaron's head and anointed him, so pouring is cited.
What is the reasoning of the one who holds that anointing is preferable?
Anointing takes precedence, as it is found with the service vessels, which were anointed without pouring.
Isn't it written that he poured and then anointed, which contradicts this view?
The verse says he poured because he had already anointed them, so anointing is primary.
Psalms 133:2 is cited about the precious oil coming down upon Aaron's beard.
Two drops of oil shaped like pearls hung from Aaron's beard, and Rav Pappa explains they rose back miraculously.
Moses worried that he had misused the consecrated oil, since two drops remained on Aaron's beard.
A Divine Voice answers Moses with Psalms 133, comparing the oil to the dew of Hermon, which is not consecrated.
Aaron, still worried, suspected that he himself had misused the consecrated oil on his beard.
A Divine Voice cites Psalms 133:1 to reassure Aaron that he, like Moses, did not misuse the oil.
A baraita teaches that kings are anointed only at a spring, so that their kingdom will flow on.
First Kings 1:33-34 is cited to show that Solomon was anointed at the spring of Gihon.
Rabbi Ami and others describe omens: a lamp that keeps burning, and a rooster that grows fat, indicate success.
One who wants to travel may test the omen of seeing the shadow of a shadow in a dark house.
The Sages reject this omen as insignificant, since a failed omen might discourage the person.
Abaye replies that omens matter, so one should accustom oneself to seeing good omens on Rosh HaShana.
Rav Mesharshiyya advises his son how to study with his teacher, starting with the baraita and attending closely.
Isaiah 30:20 is cited: your eyes shall see your teacher.
Rav Mesharshiyya advises studying by a river and sitting in the rubbish heaps of Mata Meḥasya.
First Samuel 2:1 is cited: my horn is exalted in my God.
David and Solomon were anointed with a horn and reigned long, while Saul and Jehu were anointed with a jug and did not.
The mishna asks who the anointed priest is: the High Priest anointed with the anointing oil.
A baraita explains that the term anointed excludes the king, the priest consecrated by garments, and the one anointed for war.
The verse Leviticus 6:15 says the anointed priest, which identifies the highest-ranking priest.
From where is this inferred?
As Rava explains about the thigh, the stronger of the thighs, so the anointed refers to the most distinguished.
The Master says the verse says anointed, and one might think it refers to a king.
But does a king bring a bull? No, a king brings a male goat, so why is the verse needed?
The tanna teaches that only the High Priest brings a bull, to exclude the king.
The mishna says the difference between the High Priests is only the bull for any mitzva transgression.
A baraita shows that this mishna does not follow Rabbi Meir, who requires the bull for the garment-consecrated priest.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir?
Leviticus 4:3 is read to include the priest consecrated by garments, since the verse says the anointed priest.
So in accordance with which opinion did you explain the mishna?

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The latter clause of the mishna is introduced as reaching the opinion of Rabbi Meir.
A baraita gives Rabbi Meir's view that the first High Priest returns and the second keeps priestly duties, against Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yosei recounts an incident with Yosef ben Eilim, who could serve neither as High Priest nor as ordinary priest, and why.
Can the first clause be the Rabbis' view and the latter clause Rabbi Meir's view?
Rav Ḥisda and Rav Yosef reconcile the mishna by assigning different clauses to different tanna'im.
Rava says the whole mishna is Rabbi Shimon's view, agreeing with Rabbi Meir on one point and not on another.
A baraita lists the differences between a High Priest and an ordinary priest, from the bull offering to marriage rules.
The baraita continues with the High Priest's mourning, his sharing of offerings, his eight garments, and Yom Kippur service.
Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages disagree on which halakhot apply to a priest anointed for war, and on restoring the murderer.
From where can we know that the tanna of the baraita is Rabbi Shimon?
Rav Pappa says the view that a High Priest is exempt from the sliding-scale offering is Rabbi Shimon's.
Everything applies except the five matters stated in the portion of the High Priest's laws.
Leviticus 21:10 is read to show the five matters apply to the High Priest, the anointed-for-war priest, and the garment-consecrated priest.
Leviticus 21:12 and 21:13 are read to limit the anointing-oil rule to the High Priest and to include the anointed-for-war priest.
The verse about marrying a virgin is a tanna'itic dispute, with Rabbi Yishmael's view on the inclusion.
Rabbi Akiva derives from the word 'and he' that a High Priest disqualified by blemishes must marry a virgin.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman whether an anointed High Priest with leprosy may marry a widow; Rav Pappa raises the same question.
Huna, son of Rav Naḥman, cites the baraita: 'and he' includes a High Priest disqualified by blemish such as leprosy.
Rav Pappa, pleased with Huna's learning, kisses him and gives him his daughter in marriage.
The mishna says a High Priest rends his garments from below, and an ordinary priest from above.
Rav and Shmuel differ on whether 'from below' and 'from above' mean the hem or the neckline.
A baraita about rending the neckline for a father or mother is cited against Shmuel's view.
Shmuel holds the view of Rabbi Yehuda, that a tear without rending the neckline is gratuitous.
Does Rabbi Yehuda hold that a High Priest may rend garments at all?
A baraita shows Rabbi Yehuda holds the High Priest does not rend his garments, while Rabbi Yishmael disagrees.
Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on the manner of rending but disagrees that the High Priest rends at all.
The mishna says a more frequent mitzva precedes another, and a more sanctified person precedes another.
From where are these principles derived?
Abaye derives from Numbers 28:23 that the daily offering is more frequent and so takes precedence.
The mishna restates that anyone more sanctified takes precedence over another.
From where do we derive that the more sanctified person takes precedence?
Leviticus 21:8 is read to grant the priest precedence in opening the Torah, blessing, and taking the portion.

ranges.en: The mishna asserts that the anointed priest's bull precedes the congregation's bull in all its rites.
From where are these precedence rules derived?
Leviticus 4:21 says 'the first', which teaches that the anointed priest's bull comes first in all rites.
A baraita restates that the anointed priest's bull precedes the congregation's bull in all its actions.
The reasoning: the one who atones should precede the one who receives atonement, as a matter of logic.
Leviticus 16:17 is cited: he atones for himself, his household, and the whole congregation.
A communal bull for an unwitting sin precedes a bull for idol worship, according to a baraita.
What is the reason: one is a sin-offering and the other a burnt-offering?
Leviticus 5:8 and 5:10 establish that every sin-offering precedes the burnt-offering that accompanies it.
Even a bird sin-offering precedes an animal burnt-offering, as the accepted rule holds.
A bull for idol worship brought by the congregation precedes a goat for idol worship.
Why should the goat, a sin-offering, be preferred over the bull, a burnt-offering?
Numbers 15:24 is read: 'leḥattat' lacks an alef, and 'according to the ordinance' fixes the order of the bull first.
A communal goat for idol worship precedes the king's goat, and the king's goat precedes an individual's female goat.
An individual's female goat is preferred over an individual's ewe as a standard sin-offering.
A baraita says the ewe of an individual precedes the female goat, contradicting the previous statement.
Abaye says it is a dispute between tanna'im over whether the goat or the ewe is preferable.
The omer precedes its lamb, the two loaves precede their sheep, and any day-dependent offering precedes a bread-dependent one.
The mishna says a man precedes a woman in rescue or return of lost property, while a woman precedes in clothing and release.
A baraita gives the order of release from captivity, and says a Torah scholar precedes the king of Israel.
First Kings 1:33 is cited: the king said to take the servants of his lord, showing a king precedes a High Priest.
First Kings 1:34 and Zechariah 3:8 show a High Priest precedes a prophet, and a sign means a prophet.
The anointed High Priest precedes other priests, down to the deputy High Priest and the overseer.
What is the meaning of amarkal?
Rav Ḥisda explains amarkal is a contraction of amar kulla, meaning he says it all.
The overseer precedes the treasurer, who precedes the priestly watch head, who precedes the head of a patrilineal family.
Regarding impurity, which comes first: the deputy High Priest or the priest anointed for war, when burying a met mitzva?
Mar Zutra cites a baraita that it is preferable for the priest anointed for war to become impure rather than the deputy.
But a baraita says the priest anointed for war precedes the deputy High Priest, seemingly contradicting this.
Ravina explains the baraita applies to rescuing him from danger, not to ritual impurity.
The mishna lists precedence among priest, Levite, Israelite, mamzer, Gibeonite, convert, and emancipated slave.
First Chronicles 23:13 and Deuteronomy 10:8 are cited to show priest precedes Levite and Levite precedes Israelite.
Reasons are given for each precedence: legitimacy, fit lineage, sanctified upbringing, and being included in the curse.
From where are these matters derived?
Proverbs 3:15 is cited: Torah is more precious than the High Priest entering the Holy of Holies.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai says an emancipated slave should precede a convert, but the convert precedes due to the curse.
Why does everyone run to marry a female convert, but not an emancipated Canaanite maidservant?
The maidservant was in the category of the curse, and the convert presumably retains chastity.
Why does a dog recognize its master, while a cat does not?
Eating the mouse makes the cat forget even more than eating what a mouse eats, so the cat does not recognize its owner.
Why do all predators dominate mice?
Mice have an evil inclination, as their nature is bad.
What is the indication of this?
Rava says they gnaw even at cloaks, which provide them no nourishment.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa says the ancient habit of gnawing even on the handle of a hoe is a sign of mice's nature.
A baraita lists five things that cause one to forget Torah study and five that restore it.
The Gemara supports the baraita's olive oil and wine claims by citing Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rava.
Dipping a finger in salt restores learning; Rabbi Yehuda says one finger and Rabbi Yosei says two.
A mnemonic for the dispute: the ring finger, kemitza.
A baraita lists ten things that are detrimental to Torah study, such as passing between camels or women.
A baraita sets the rules for how people stand and seat themselves when the Nasi, deputy Nasi, or Ḥakham enters.
A baraita rules on how sons of Torah scholars sit before their fathers, depending on whether they can hear and study.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok adds that at a wedding party such youths are seated next to their fathers.
Rav Pappa limits the return to one's place to a man who left for minor bodily functions.
Rav Pappa cites Rav Yehuda's teaching in Rav's name: one should train oneself to relieve oneself morning and evening.
Rava says that in weak times one may return even after major bodily functions, and repeats the rule about wedding parties.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the baraita was taught in the days of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who sought to distinguish himself.
When Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan returned, they found the new deference rules had been instituted in their absence.
Rabbi Meir proposes that they test Rabban Shimon by asking him to teach tractate Okatzin, which he does not know.
Rabbi Ya'akov ben Korshei overhears the plan and warns it may humiliate Rabban Shimon, so he studies Okatzin quietly.
Rabban Shimon suspects a plot, studies Okatzin, and then teaches it, saying he would have been humiliated otherwise.
Rabban Shimon has Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan expelled from the study hall as punishment.
Rabbi Yosei asks the Sages how the Torah embodied in preeminent scholars is outside while the Sages are inside.
Rabban Shimon agrees to readmit them with penalties, and the Rabbis later recall Rabbi Natan's dream and appeasement.

ranges.en: The passage continues the baraita: a substitute animal would not be sacrificed, citing the rule about the Sages' view.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son asks who the Sages are whose water we drink but whose names we do not mention.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replies that they sought to abolish his honor and the honor of his father's house.
The son cites Ecclesiastes 9:6 to argue that since they are long dead, their names may be mentioned.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi counters with Psalms 9:7: though enemies die, the desolation they caused remains.
Rabban Shimon says the rule applies where their actions were effective, and these Sages' actions were not.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches the Sages' view in Rabbi Meir's name, and Rava notes his humility in not citing Rabbi Meir directly.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis disagreed on whether Sinai or uprooter of mountains is preferable.
Rav Yosef, the Sinai type, and Rabba, the mountain-uprooter, exchanged messages, with Rabba reigning before Rav Yosef.
Abaye, Rava, Rabbi Zeira and Rabba bar Mattana study together, and Abaye's statement is the one not refuted, so he leads.
A dilemma is raised: which of Rabbi Zeira and Rabba bar Rav Mattana is preferable?
Rabbi Zeira is incisive and raises difficulties, while Rabba bar Rav Mattana is moderate and reaches conclusions.
The Gemara concludes: the dilemma stands unresolved.
The colophon concludes the chapter beginning Kohen Mashiaḥ and the tractate of Horayot.
